title: A simulation grows early black holes from heavy seeds
freshness: Published in Nature on 16 September 2026, within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
excerpt: Webb keeps finding giant black holes, and compact red sources called little red dots, at times when a stellar-mass seed growing at a modest rate should not yet be huge. A Nature simulation grows heavy seeds from unusually massive first stars, lets them feed furiously for a short time, and produces objects that look like those dots.
whyItMatters: The early black holes are an observational problem: they look too big, too soon. This paper is a simulation, not a detection of the first stars. It shows one route by which heavy seeds in dense gas can front-load their growth and leave compact red sources, if the massive stars at the start are granted.

exploreFurther.label: Nature: Overmassive black holes and little red dots naturally form in simulations

whatToExploreNext: Little red dots: compact, reddish sources Webb found that may be an early, dust-hidden stage of supermassive black hole growth.
body:
## Too big, too soon

Giant black holes show up early. Webb finds them, and finds the compact red sources called little red dots, at times when a black hole that started near the mass of a star and then ate at a polite rate should not yet be enormous. A Nature paper published on 16 September 2026 reports a simulation in which the early universe grows those objects anyway. The route is short. Unusually massive first stars collapse into large black-hole seeds. Those seeds then grow extremely quickly for a brief time. The output looks like the little red dots.

The title's word for the black holes is "overmassive," meaning too heavy for how little time the young universe had given them. The title also says the overmassive black holes and the little red dots form naturally in the simulations. "Naturally" is the authors' claim that the dots and the heavy black holes come out of the run, rather than being painted on at the end. The seeds and the dense gas are the setup. The quick growth and the compact red appearance are what the run produces.

The method matters more than the headline. This is a simulation. It is not a spectrum of a named object. It is not a detection of a first-generation star. The Nature article is the only source attached here. There is no separate observatory release to lean on. The page is the journal article itself, and the account below stays inside what that public summary already supports.

## Heavy seeds, then a short feast

A seed, in this context, is the black hole left behind when a star collapses. It is the starting mass for everything that comes later. If the first stars are unusually massive, the black holes they leave are large from the start. You do not have to grow a stellar-mass remnant into a giant. You start partway there.

"Unusually" is doing a lot of quiet work. Getting first stars that heavy, inside a simulation, means choosing how their birth clouds behave. The choices that carry the result are less fine fragmentation, rapid accretion of the surrounding gas, and a different cooling history in metal-free clouds. Those are settings in the run. They are not new observations of a named first star delivered by this paper. Grant them, and the channel opens. Refuse them, and this particular route stays shut.

The second piece is a short episode of very fast growth. A seed buried in dense gas can pull material in furiously until the gas is cleared or the supply thins. In that window the black hole gains mass at a rate that looks outrageous next to a later galaxy where gas is scarce. The window ends. You do not need the black hole to eat at that rate for a billion years. You need the furious stretch early, while the surroundings are still thick. Front-loading is the whole trick. A polite rate, held for a long time, is the schedule that fails to finish. A heavy start plus a brief feast is the schedule the simulation uses instead.

## What "looks like a little red dot" means

Little red dots, as Webb finds them, are compact and red. They are easier to explain if a lot of the light is tied to a growing black hole than if it comes from a mature galaxy of ordinary stars. The simulation's objects come out similar: compact, red, and in that same interpretive neighborhood. Similarity is a comparison the authors are offering. It is not an identification of any particular dot in a Webb catalog. No dot is named. No redshift is claimed here. No mass is copied off a spectrum.

A mock population can resemble a real class without any mock object being the same as a catalogued dot. The useful statement is narrower. Given heavy seeds and dense early gas, a run can produce compact red sources and black holes already too heavy for a slow-growth story. The dots remain the clue. The run is one way to produce that clue without breaking the timeline.

## A channel, not a catch

A separate observed source, MoM-BH*-1, has been discussed as a black hole wrapped in a dense gas cocoon, and as a possible example of the kind of object a little red dot might be. That discussion is a spectrum and a fit to a real source. This Nature paper is a formation channel that could supply the black holes such dots might contain. The two results rhyme. They are not the same evidence. One starts from light collected from the sky. The other starts from a setup and grows a mock population.

If the channel works, the timing problem is less severe: the seeds were never small, and the growth spurt was loaded into the beginning. If the first stars were not that massive, the channel does not open, and the problem stands where Webb left it. Rapid growth falls out of a dense early environment only once the heavy seeds are granted. Granting them is the interpretive step.

The claim to keep is a possible route, not a discovery of heavy seeds in the sky. The run produced compact, red objects from seeds left by unusually massive first stars after a short interval of extremely fast growth. It did not detect a first star, name a dot, or prove that nature used this route. The Nature article is the authority for what the simulation included. The dots are still the clue in the data.
